options.text: The flow of electric charge through a conductor
options.feedback: Correct -- current measures how much charge moves past a point per unit time.

options.text: The resistance in a wire

medium.text: In what unit is electric current typically measured?

options.text: Amperes (amps)
options.feedback: Correct -- amperes measure the rate of electric charge flow.

options.text: Volts
options.feedback: Volts measure electric potential difference (voltage), not current.

options.text: Ohms
options.feedback: Ohms measure electrical resistance, not current.

options.text: Watts
options.feedback: Watts measure power, a different (though related) electrical quantity.

hard.text: In a simple circuit, electrons actually flow from the negative terminal to the positive terminal of the battery, but conventional current is defined as flowing in the opposite direction. Why?

options.text: Conventional current direction was historically defined before electrons were discovered, based on the assumed flow of positive charge
options.feedback: Correct -- early scientists defined current direction based on positive charge flow, and that convention stuck even after electrons (negative charges) were later discovered.

options.text: Electrons don't actually move in a circuit at all
options.feedback: Electrons do physically move through the conductor -- this scenario is about the historical labeling convention, not actual electron movement.

options.text: Positive charges physically flow in real circuits, not electrons
options.feedback: In most everyday circuits, it's electrons that physically move, even though conventional current is labeled the opposite way.

options.text: This is simply a modern printing error found in most textbooks
options.feedback: This is an intentional, historically established scientific convention, not an error.

easy.hard: This describes the motion of charged particles moving through a wire or circuit.
easy.medium: This describes charged particles moving through a conducting path.
easy.easy: This is the flow of electricity through a wire.

medium.hard: This unit is named after a pioneering French physicist and measures charge flow rate.
medium.medium: This unit is often abbreviated with the letter 'A.'

easy.text: According to the law of conservation of energy, energy can be:

options.text: Transformed from one form to another, but not created or destroyed
options.feedback: Correct -- total energy in a closed system remains constant, even as it changes form.

options.text: Created out of nothing whenever needed
options.feedback: Energy cannot be created from nothing -- it must come from another form of energy already present.

options.text: Completely destroyed after use
options.feedback: Energy isn't destroyed -- it transforms into other forms, like heat or motion.

options.text: Only stored, never used
options.feedback: Stored energy can definitely be used and converted into other forms, like motion or heat.

medium.text: A swinging pendulum slows down over time due to air resistance and friction. According to conservation of energy, where does the 'lost' mechanical energy go?

options.text: It converts into heat energy released into the surroundings
options.feedback: Correct -- friction and air resistance convert mechanical energy into heat, which then disperses into the environment.

options.text: It simply disappears and ceases to exist
options.feedback: Energy is never truly destroyed -- it transforms into another form, in this case heat.

options.text: It transfers entirely into the pendulum's mass
options.feedback: Mass doesn't increase from this process -- the energy converts into heat, not into added mass.

options.text: It converts into additional gravitational potential energy
options.feedback: The pendulum's swings actually get smaller over time, meaning its potential energy decreases, not increases.

hard.text: A ball is dropped from a height and bounces repeatedly, reaching a lower height with each bounce. What does this observation demonstrate about the collisions with the ground?

options.text: Each collision is not perfectly elastic -- some mechanical energy converts to heat and sound with each bounce
options.feedback: Correct -- real-world collisions lose some mechanical energy to heat and sound, which is why the bounce height decreases each time.

options.text: Energy is being created with each bounce
options.feedback: The ball's energy is decreasing over time, not increasing -- energy isn't being created here.

options.text: Gravity gets weaker after each bounce
options.feedback: Gravity's strength doesn't change during this process -- the ball's total mechanical energy is what's decreasing.

options.text: The ball's mass increases with each bounce
options.feedback: The ball's mass stays constant -- the decreasing bounce height reflects energy loss, not mass change.

easy.hard: Energy simply changes its form -- it never appears from nothing or vanishes into nothing.
easy.medium: Energy just changes form -- it doesn't vanish or appear out of nowhere.
easy.easy: Energy doesn't disappear -- it just changes into a different form.

medium.hard: Friction and air resistance are classic mechanisms that convert organized mechanical motion into disordered thermal energy.
medium.medium: Friction and air resistance turn the pendulum's motion energy into heat that spreads into the air.
medium.easy: The pendulum's motion energy turns into heat due to friction and air resistance.

hard.hard: A perfectly elastic collision would preserve all kinetic energy and result in the same bounce height every time -- the decreasing height reveals ongoing energy loss to heat and sound at each impact.
hard.medium: Since the ball keeps bouncing lower and lower, some energy must be leaking out as heat and sound with every bounce.
hard.easy: Since the bounces get smaller, some energy is being lost as heat and sound each time it hits the ground.

options.text: How quickly work is done
options.feedback: Correct -- power is the rate at which work is performed or energy is transferred.

options.text: The total distance an object travels
options.feedback: Distance alone doesn't capture how fast work is being done -- that's what power measures.

options.text: The color of the energy source
options.feedback: Color has no bearing on the physics definition of power.

options.text: The weight of an object
options.feedback: Weight is a separate quantity, unrelated to the rate of doing work.

medium.text: If 100 joules of work is done in 5 seconds, what is the power?

options.text: 20 watts
options.feedback: Correct -- power equals work divided by time: 100÷5=20.

options.text: 500 watts
options.feedback: This multiplies instead of dividing work by time.

options.text: 95 watts
options.feedback: This subtracts instead of dividing work by time.

options.text: 105 watts
options.feedback: This adds instead of dividing work by time.

hard.text: Two machines each lift the same 500 N load to the same height, but Machine A does it in 10 seconds while Machine B takes 20 seconds. What can you conclude?

options.text: Machine A has twice the power output of Machine B
options.feedback: Correct -- with equal work done in half the time, Machine A's power (work/time) is double Machine B's.

options.text: Machine B did more total work than Machine A
options.feedback: Both machines did the exact same amount of total work -- lifting the same load the same height -- only the time differed.

options.text: Machine A used less energy overall than Machine B
options.feedback: Both machines used the same amount of energy (work) -- the difference is only in how fast that work was completed.

options.text: Power output was identical for both machines
options.feedback: Since Machine A completed the same work in half the time, its power output must be higher, not identical.

easy.hard: This quantity relates the amount of work accomplished to the time it took to accomplish it.
easy.medium: This tells you how fast energy is being transferred or work is being done.
easy.easy: This tells you how quickly work gets done.

medium.hard: Divide the amount of work performed by the time taken to perform it.
medium.medium: Divide 100 by 5 to find the power.

hard.medium: Since the work is the same for both, the machine that took less time must have a higher power output.
hard.easy: Since Machine A did the same job in half the time, it must be twice as powerful.

easy.text: What is the main benefit of using an inclined plane (ramp) to move a heavy object?

options.text: It reduces the amount of force needed, spread over a longer distance
options.feedback: Correct -- a ramp trades a longer travel distance for a smaller required force.

options.text: It makes the object weigh less
options.feedback: An inclined plane doesn't change an object's actual weight, just how much force is needed to move it.

options.text: It eliminates the need for any force at all
options.feedback: Some force is still required to move an object up a ramp -- it's just less than lifting it straight up.

options.text: It speeds up the object automatically
options.feedback: An inclined plane's main benefit is reducing force needed, not automatically increasing speed.

medium.text: Comparing a short, steep ramp to a long, gently sloped ramp for lifting the same object to the same height, which requires less force?

options.text: The long, gently sloped ramp
options.feedback: Correct -- a longer ramp spreads the same work over a greater distance, reducing the force needed at any point.

options.text: The short, steep ramp
options.feedback: A steeper, shorter ramp actually requires more force since the same height gain happens over less distance.

options.text: Both ramps require exactly the same force
options.feedback: The force needed changes with the ramp's length and steepness -- they aren't the same in this comparison.

options.text: Neither ramp requires any force
options.feedback: Moving an object up any ramp against gravity always requires some force.

hard.text: A ramp is 10 meters long and rises to a height of 2 meters. If lifting the load straight up would require 100 N of force, approximately how much force is needed to push it up the ramp (ignoring friction)?

options.feedback: Correct -- using the ramp's mechanical advantage (length÷height = 10÷2 = 5), the force needed is 100÷5=20 N.
This ignores the mechanical advantage the ramp provides.
This multiplies instead of dividing by the ramp's mechanical advantage.
This doesn't correctly use the ramp's length-to-height ratio.

easy.hard: This trade-off exchanges a smaller effort force for having to apply that force over more distance.
easy.medium: You push with less force, but you have to push the object over a longer path.
easy.easy: You need less force, but you have to push the object farther.

medium.hard: A longer ramp achieves the same height gain more gradually, spreading the required work over more distance and thus requiring less force at any moment.
medium.medium: The longer ramp spreads the same height gain over more distance, so it takes less force to push something up it.
medium.easy: The longer, gentler ramp needs less pushing force since it covers more distance to reach the same height.

hard.hard: Divide the straight-lift force by the ramp's mechanical advantage, calculated as the ramp's length divided by its height.
hard.medium: Divide the ramp's length by its height to find the mechanical advantage, then divide the straight-lift force by that number.
hard.easy: Divide 10 by 2 to get 5, then divide 100 by 5 to find the force needed.

topic: sound requires a medium to travel

easy.text: Sound waves need what in order to travel from one place to another?

options.text: A medium, such as air, water, or a solid
options.feedback: Correct -- sound is a mechanical wave that requires particles of matter to transmit its vibrations.

options.text: Complete darkness
options.feedback: Darkness or light has no effect on whether sound can travel.

options.text: Nothing at all -- it can travel through empty space
options.feedback: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum -- it needs particles of matter to carry its vibrations.

options.text: Extremely high temperatures
options.feedback: Sound doesn't require high temperatures -- it just needs some medium of matter to travel through.

medium.text: Why can astronauts not hear explosions directly in the vacuum of space?

options.text: There are no particles of matter in a vacuum to carry the sound vibrations
options.feedback: Correct -- without air or any other matter, there's nothing for the sound wave to travel through.

options.text: Explosions in space don't produce any sound energy at all
options.feedback: The explosion does produce vibrations, but with no matter present, those vibrations have nothing to travel through.

options.text: Astronauts' spacesuits completely block all sound
options.feedback: The core issue is the vacuum itself lacking any medium, not the suit blocking sound.

options.text: Sound travels too fast in space to be detected
options.feedback: Sound doesn't travel through a vacuum at all, regardless of speed -- there's no medium to carry it.

hard.text: Sound generally travels faster through solids than through air. Why?

options.text: Particles in a solid are packed closer together, transmitting vibrations more quickly between neighbors
options.feedback: Correct -- tightly packed solid particles pass vibrational energy to each other faster than the more spread-out particles in air.

options.text: Solids are always colder than air, and cold speeds up sound
options.feedback: Temperature isn't the main factor here -- particle spacing and how tightly they interact is what matters most.

options.text: Sound doesn't actually travel through solids at all
options.feedback: Sound does travel through solids -- often faster than through air or liquids.

options.text: Solids have no mass, so sound moves instantly through them
options.feedback: Solids definitely have mass -- their particle arrangement, not lack of mass, explains the faster sound speed.

easy.hard: This kind of wave physically pushes and pulls particles of matter to propagate.
easy.medium: This wave type needs particles of some kind of matter to bump into each other and pass the vibration along.
easy.easy: Sound needs some kind of matter -- like air or water -- to travel through.

medium.hard: This environment lacks any particles of matter whatsoever for a mechanical wave to propagate through.
medium.medium: This environment has no air or any other matter at all for sound to travel through.
medium.easy: Space is basically empty, with no air or matter for sound to travel through.

hard.hard: Closer particle spacing in solids allows faster transfer of vibrational energy from particle to neighboring particle compared to the more dispersed particles in a gas.
hard.medium: In a solid, particles are packed much closer together, so vibrations can pass from one to the next more quickly.
hard.easy: Solid particles are packed tightly together, so the vibration passes between them faster than in air.
